lyrics:
What a lovely woman…
There’s the glance
There’s the second glance
There’s the third one you disguise
As a sudden deep concern about
The exit sign behind her eyes
Then the posture
Then the coughing
Then the fascinating floor
Nothing makes a grown man study grout
Like what he noticed four feet before
Peripheral
Accidental
Purely educational
Two whole seconds later—
deeply constitutional
Hey boob Shirley
Why you staring at me
Hey boob Shirley
They’re real, naturally
It’s all about reaction
A stunning self reflection
It’s primal
Compelling
Flatly overwhelming
So don’t pretend that you don’t want
the attention that you crave
Don’t just free them partly
Free the whole thing
First you cover for the weather
Then you decorate the hide
Tie a shell around the ankle
put a little color on the side
Raise it
Shape it
Paint it
Pad it
Make a feature where you had it
If the signal gets attention
then the signal gets repeated
And it worked
Somewhere back before the fitting room
before the label, before the brand
somebody added something extra
and somebody else said
“Damn.”
Decorative
Competitive
Highly reproductive
Slightly exaggerated—
surprisingly effective
Hey boob Shirley
Why you staring at me
Hey boob Shirley
Checking out the competition, I see
It’s all about reaction
A little self-comparison
It’s primal
Compelling
Flatly overwhelming
You can call it taste
or fashion
or whatever keeps you brave
But if beauty wasn’t working
we’d have stopped it
in the cave
Don’t just free them partly
Free the whole thing
So there you have it
A little color
A little lift
A little something nature
apparently forgot to gift
Three beats for displaying
Two beats for the scan
Nobody wrote the handbook—
but everybody understands
You can call it presentation
You can call it social art
But somewhere underneath the tailoring
the monkey got a head start

And apparently
he brought accessories

HEY BOOB SHIRLEY
Why you staring at me
HEY BOOB SHIRLEY
Checking out the competition, I see
It’s all about reaction
Mutual inspection
It’s primal
Compelling
Flatly overwhelming
You can dress it up as culture
You can file it under taste
But biology keeps peeking
through the buttons at the waist
So don’t pretend that you don’t want
the attention that you crave
Don’t just free them partly
Free the whole thing
(Free the whole thing.)
(The whole thing.)
Yes, Shirley
We noticed

So after several thousand generations
of feathers
beads
buckles
buttons
padding
plunging necklines
raised heels
lowered hems
raised hems
and the occasional strategically placed shiny object
we have reached
the highly advanced conclusion
that people enjoy being looked at—
provided they approve
of who is looking
And the rest of us
will continue pretending
we were reading the exit sign

Nice grout, by the way

  Approved critic summary: "A Distant Memory" opens with a counted-off "one, two, three, four" that sets a brisk 4/4 in C major, and from there Rose lets a female vocal float above a clean, roomy groove that leans more toward jazzy indie-pop than any straight ballad.

  Approved critic summary: There's a bat by the bed in this one, his father's before him, and nobody in the family has ever swung it.

  Approved critic summary: Nearly seven minutes, and Rose earns every one of them here by treating silence itself as the subject.

  Approved critic summary: For a songwriter introduced as a diarist, a philosopher of the ordinary who finds a lifetime in a reflection on a phone screen, "Outlandia" is a startling pivot: a two-hour rock opera, twenty-four scenes long, about how a country is bought, broken, and inventoried.

  Approved critic summary: After the two-hour sprawl of "Outlandia," Rose narrows the lens back down to something you can hold in one hand, and "Them Bones" benefits from the compression.

  Approved critic summary: Rose builds this one on a 3/4 pulse at a brisk clip, which is the first surprise: a waltz that never asks you to sway, driven instead by a Hammond groove and gritty guitar working against the meter rather than settling into it.

impression.text: This highly theatrical track bursts with a playful, comedic, and slightly sarcastic emotional atmosphere. The energy level remains exceptionally high and dynamic throughout the piece, driven by punchy orchestral hits and sharp start-and-stop rhythmic arrangements. Production is incredibly dense yet meticulously balanced, allowing snappy brass, sweeping strings, and quirky percussion to sit perfectly around the charismatic narrative lead vocal. A defining quality of the track is its rapid-fire storytelling delivery which synchronizes flawlessly with the exaggerated Broadway-style instrumentation and sudden dramatic pauses.

review.review_text: The comedy here isn't in spite of the craft, it's built from it. Rose sets a marimba walking figure loose over a broken-waltz pulse at a brisk 136, and the arrangement earns its jokes with timing: the stop-start accents on 'Peripheral. Accidental. Purely educational' land like a man caught red-handed, and the whole thing pivots on that guilty deadpan of a grown man who'll 'study grout / Like what he noticed four feet before.' The mock-anthropology of verse two ('First you cover for the weather. Then you decorate the hide') is where the writing sharpens into something Randy Newman would recognize, an unreliable narrator dressing up base instinct as social theory. The 5/4 instrumental break is the record's real flex, marimba restating the motif in a 3+2 stagger while the flute exaggerates the strut and the guitar answers crooked, before the final bar snaps abruptly back to a straight-4/4 chorus. If the bit runs slightly long, the outro's catalog of 'feathers, beads, buckles, buttons' testing your patience before the final 'Nice grout, by the way' pays it off, the way a good closing line pays off a shaggy joke. A highlight, and proof Rose can make a novelty conceit hold real musical weight.
